title: Climbing Ama Dablam: Full Guide
excerpt: Ama Dablam, 6,812 m, is a technical summit in the Everest region. The full guide: the southwest ridge, the camps, the Yellow Tower, fixed ropes, acclimatization, permits and cost.
seoTitle: Climbing Ama Dablam: Route, Camps, Experience and Cost

content.value: On leaving Camp 1, at about 5,700 m, climbers clip into the first fixed rope, and from there the way to the summit of Ama Dablam, 6,812 m (22,349 ft), runs along fixed ropes. Ama Dablam is a technical summit in the Khumbu region of Nepal, close to Everest, and its route climbs the southwest ridge, combining rock, ice and mixed climbing with exposed passages. It requires good fitness, previous technical climbing experience and adaptation to altitude, and it suits experienced climbers. Its main season is the fall, and with us it is a 30-day expedition that departs in October.

Its sharp shape has earned it the nickname "the Matterhorn of the Himalayas", and anyone who has walked the Everest Base Camp trek remembers it well: it rises above the trail for several days of walking. Climbing it is another matter altogether. Here is what you need to know before you decide: our expedition day by day, the rotations and acclimatization, the Yellow Tower and the upper ridge, the gear, the experience required and the price.
The Matterhorn of the Himalayas

Ama Dablam rises in the Khumbu valley of eastern Nepal, within Sagarmatha National Park, above the village of Pangboche and not far from Everest and Lhotse. Its name, "Mother's Necklace", comes from the hanging glacier on its flanks, which looks like a pendant on a mother's neck. A dablam is a traditional Sherpa pendant, and ama is the mother.

Most climbers go up the southwest ridge, and that is also the route of our expedition. Unlike summits where the technical part is concentrated on a single wall, here the whole ridge is technical: granite slabs and rock towers, snowy ledges, a narrow snow ridge and a steep slope of snow and ice at the end. For most of the way above Camp 1 climbers move clipped to a rope, and the exposure is considerable. We grade the climb as extreme, the highest grade on our difficulty scale.
Our expedition, day by day
The HighAir Ama Dablam expedition lasts 30 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. The altitudes in brackets are those of the overnight stop or of the high point of that day:

items: Day 1: arrival in Kathmandu and transfer to the hotel.
Day 2: preparation day and gear check in Kathmandu.
Day 3: flight to Lukla and a walk to Phakding (2,610 m).
Day 4: up to Namche Bazaar (3,440 m).
Day 5: acclimatization day in Namche Bazaar.
Day 8: up to Ama Dablam Base Camp (4,600 m).
Day 9: preparation and rest day at Base Camp.
Day 10: puja ceremony and the start of the climbing rotations.
Days 11 to 20: rotations and acclimatization at the high camps.
Day 21: summit push to Ama Dablam (6,812 m) and descent to sleep at Camp 2.
Day 22: descent from Camp 2 to Base Camp.
Days 23 to 25: spare days for weather, at Base Camp.
Day 26: down to Namche Bazaar (3,440 m).
Day 27: the last walking day, to Lukla (2,860 m).
Day 28: flight from Lukla to Kathmandu or Ramechhap.
Day 29: spare day in case of bad weather, or a free day in Kathmandu.
Day 30: transfer to the airport and flight home.

content.value: The itinerary is built in three stages. In the first, you walk up the Khumbu valley to Base Camp at a pace that leaves time to acclimatize. In the second, from day 10 to day 20, you climb up and down between Base Camp and the high camps in rotations. The third stage is the summit attempt, the descent and the way back to Lukla. In all you spend 18 nights at Base Camp and the camps above it.

content.title: ✦ Room to wait for the weather
content.value: The itinerary has three spare days at Base Camp, days 23 to 25, set aside for bad weather, and one more spare day in Kathmandu before the flight home. If wind or snow closes the mountain on the planned date, there is room to wait for a better window.
The way in: the Khumbu valley

The expedition starts in Lukla, 2,860 m, the village that is home to the airport of the Everest region. The flights from Kathmandu to Lukla and back are by plane, and they are included in the price. They depend on the weather, and in the busy seasons many of them leave from the airport at Manthali in Ramechhap district, a few hours' drive from Kathmandu. In our itinerary the return flight from Lukla lands in Kathmandu or Ramechhap, and day 29 is a spare day in case it is delayed.

From Lukla you walk up the Dudh Koshi river valley to Phakding and Namche Bazaar, the Sherpa market town, and stay there for an acclimatization day. From there you continue to Deboche, near Tengboche monastery, and to Pangboche, the village from which you climb to Ama Dablam Base Camp. Along the trek you sleep in teahouses in twin rooms, and three meals a day, chosen from the menu, are included in the price. The large bag, up to 15 kg per person, is carried by the porters, and you walk with a daypack. Internet, laundry and extra meals at the teahouses are not included, so bring some cash for them.
As far as Pangboche the way follows the trail of the Everest Base Camp trek, and we have written a complete guide to it, describing the stages, life in the teahouses and the flight to Lukla.

content.value: Base Camp and the puja ceremony

On day 8 you climb from Pangboche to Ama Dablam Base Camp, 4,600 m, an open grassy flat at the foot of the mountain. From here on you sleep in twin tents, both at Base Camp and at the high camps, and the three meals a day continue throughout the climb. Day 9 is set aside for preparation and rest.

At Base Camp you go through technical training with professional guides before heading up the ridge. Every climber on the expedition has a personal Sherpa guide, on a one-to-one ratio, who accompanies them to the summit.

On day 10 the puja is held, a traditional Buddhist ceremony asking the mountain for safe passage. A lama from one of the villages or monasteries in the area comes up to Base Camp and reads prayers in front of a small stone altar, the chorten, with colorful prayer flags strung above it. Climbers and Sherpas throw rice, and often bring their climbing gear to be blessed as well. For the Sherpas it is an inseparable part of the climb, and only after the ceremony does anyone start up the mountain.

content.value: Rotations and acclimatization

Altitude is the first challenge on Ama Dablam, even before the climbing. The higher you go, the less oxygen each breath brings in, and the body needs time to adapt. The accepted rule in mountain medicine is that above 3,000 m you do not raise your sleeping altitude by more than 500 m a night, and you add a night of acclimatization for every 1,000 m of sleeping altitude gained. For some climbers even this pace is too fast, so listen to your body.

On the mountain itself, acclimatization happens in rounds, the rotations. The principle is "climb high, sleep low": you go up to a high camp, sometimes to carry gear there and sometimes to sleep there, and come back down to Base Camp to rest and recover. Each rotation takes the body higher, and only once it has adapted do you set out on the summit attempt.

With us, ten days of the itinerary, days 11 to 20, are dedicated to rotations and acclimatization at the high camps. As with the whole route, they may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides on the ground.

Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. When symptoms get worse despite rest at the same altitude, you descend. Every group carries a pulse oximeter and a Magnus satellite device. In the mountains there is no promise of reaching the summit, but there is always a commitment to safety above all.

content.alt: Yellow tents scattered among rocks and snow on a mountain ridge, above clouds and snowy peaks
content.caption: A tent camp on a rocky, snowy ridge, above the clouds

content.value: The ridge, camp by camp

Above Base Camp you climb to Camp 1 and Camp 2, and from there to the upper part of the mountain. The fixed ropes are put up anew each season, and with us the fixing of ropes along the route to the summit is included in the price.
From Base Camp to Camp 1

The way to Camp 1 takes several hours, and in its last part you cross a field of large boulders. Camp 1 sits at about 5,700 m, at the foot of the southwest ridge, and its tents are pitched on platforms between the rocks. On leaving it you clip into the fixed ropes, and from here the real climbing begins.
The Yellow Tower and Camp 2

From Camp 1 you move along rocky and snowy ledges, over granite slabs and across exposed traverses, clipped to the rope the whole time. The hardest section comes just below Camp 2: the Yellow Tower, a steep granite tower that is the main technical section of the ridge. Most climbers go up it with a jumar, an ascender that locks onto the fixed rope and is attached to the harness, and at almost 6,000 m every meter of it takes strength in the arms and many breaths.

content.alt: A climber in a white helmet and orange jacket climbing a steep rock slab while holding fixed ropes, with snowy peaks behind
content.caption: Climbing a steep rock slab, close to the fixed ropes

content.value: Camp 2 sits on top of the Yellow Tower, at about 6,000 m, on narrow platforms with room for only a few tents, surrounded by cliffs. In our itinerary it is the camp you descend to for the night at the end of summit day.
Above Camp 2: the Gray Tower and the Mushroom Ridge

Above Camp 2 you continue to the Gray Tower, and after it to the Mushroom Ridge, a narrow, corniced snow ridge that links the rocky ridge with the upper snowfields. The exposure here is great, and movement is slow and careful. Above it you climb snow and ice fields, not far from the hanging glacier that gave the mountain its name, and finally a steep slope that eases toward the summit. The summit itself is relatively broad, and from it you look out over Everest, Lhotse and the whole Khumbu valley.
Summit day and the descent

On day 21 you set out for the summit, 6,812 m. Many expeditions leave for the summit from Camp 2 in the dark, by headlamp, so as to have time to go up and come down in daylight. It is a long, cold day, and the upper part of the route is exposed to the wind. In our itinerary you descend at the end of it to sleep at Camp 2, and on day 22 you continue to Base Camp.

The summit is only halfway. The steep sections are mostly descended by rappelling on the fixed rope, with a descender attached to the harness, and at each anchor you move from rope to rope, always clipped in. Fatigue on the descent is one of the greatest dangers in the mountains, so it is important to reach the summit with enough strength and time in hand to come down safely. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and safety comes before the summit.

content.alt: A climber in an orange jacket walking along a narrow, sharp snow ridge, an orange rope trailing behind, facing snowy peaks and clouds
content.caption: On a narrow snow ridge, clipped to the rope

content.value: Technical gear and training

On the ridge you work with a full set of climbing gear: harness, helmet, crampons, ice axe, a jumar for ascending the rope and a descender for rappelling. Personal gear, meaning clothing, footwear and climbing equipment, is not included in the price, and a full gear list is sent to every registrant after registration. The most important item is a pair of high-altitude mountaineering boots that take crampons and keep your feet warm in the cold of the high camps.

The technical training at Base Camp is part of the preparation, but it is no substitute for previous technical climbing experience, which is a requirement for this climb. It is worth arriving when the movements are already familiar to your hands: ascending on a jumar, rappelling, changing ropes at an anchor and moving in crampons on rock and ice. On the ridge, at this altitude and in the cold, there is no time to learn the basics.
Before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call.
Permits, visa and insurance

To climb Ama Dablam you need a climbing permit from the authorities in Nepal, as well as entry permits for Sagarmatha National Park and the area. The price of the climbing permit depends on the season and changes from time to time. With us the climbing permit and the entry permits for the protected areas are included in the price of the expedition, so there is no need to deal with them separately.

Most visitors, including UK, EU, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, get a Nepal tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. For a 30-day trip you need the 30-day visa, which costs 50 US dollars (as of 2026) and is not included. Travel and medical insurance is not included either. Before buying a policy, check that it covers climbing up to 6,812 m, including rescue and helicopter evacuation, and check your government's current travel advice for Nepal before you go.
When to climb Ama Dablam

Nepal has two main climbing seasons: spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. On Ama Dablam the fall is the busier season, partly because in spring many Sherpas and expedition teams are busy on Everest.

Our expedition departs in October, when the monsoon rains are already over. In this season the air is usually clear and the views open, but the nights at the high camps are very cold, so prepare your gear accordingly.
Who it suits

Ama Dablam is not a first summit. The climb requires good fitness, previous technical climbing experience and adaptation to altitude, and it suits experienced climbers looking for a genuine technical challenge in the Himalaya. A good way to gain that experience is a lower technical summit such as Island Peak, 6,189 m, where you climb a steep wall at the end of a glacier on a jumar. We have written a complete guide to it.

content.value: Ama Dablam is also a step on the way to higher summits. Anyone who has climbed its ridge, done the rotations between the camps and spent nights in a tent at about 6,000 m comes away with experience that serves as a foundation for peaks of 7,000 and 8,000 m. At HighAir the next step could be Himlung Himal, 7,126 m, and later Manaslu, 8,163 m, a summit above 8,000 m.

A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join. The best preparation is months of training: long uphill hikes with a heavy pack, strength and endurance training, and practice climbing and working with ropes at a climbing gym or on rock.

Good to know: the expedition is led by professional local guides who speak English, and every climber has a personal Sherpa guide. Come with enough English to follow instructions on the ground, including on the ridge. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and the route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides.
What it costs and what is included

The Ama Dablam expedition costs 7,000 US dollars per person. It includes transfers between the airport and the hotel in Kathmandu, dinners at a restaurant before and after the climb, 4 nights in a 4-star hotel in Kathmandu with breakfast, domestic flights to Lukla and back, teahouse accommodation in shared rooms along the trek and twin tents at Base Camp and the high camps, all entry permits for the trek and the Ama Dablam climbing permit, three meals a day from the menu, 2 liters of hot water a day, a shower and attached toilet where available on the route, a personal Sherpa guide on a one-to-one ratio all the way to the summit, technical training at Base Camp with professional guides, fixed ropes along the route to the summit, professional local English-speaking guides, porters for personal gear up to 15 kg per person, a first aid kit carried by the guides, a pulse oximeter for the group and a satellite device, a personal area in the HighAir app, a personal gear checklist with an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide, and a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance, lunch and dinner at the hotel in Kathmandu, personal gear and climbing equipment, the Nepal visa (50 dollars), tips for guides and porters (350 dollars per person), a summit bonus for the guides (800 dollars per person), vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and the extras the teahouses charge for separately, such as internet, laundry, alcohol and additional meals. A fifth hotel night in Kathmandu, if needed, is not included.
Note that in the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber.
Ama Dablam with HighAir

At HighAir we go to Ama Dablam in October, on a 30-day expedition, in groups of up to 10 climbers, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 65 percent. Our itinerary is built around patient acclimatization: an acclimatization day in Namche Bazaar, a rest day at Base Camp, ten days of rotations, three spare days on the mountain and one more in Kathmandu. A personal Sherpa guide climbs beside every climber.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber who stands on a summit like Ama Dablam got there mountain by mountain, and step by step. If your first technical summits are already behind you and Ama Dablam is next, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does it take to climb Ama Dablam?

The HighAir expedition lasts 30 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. About a week is spent walking up the Khumbu valley to Base Camp, ten days are dedicated to rotations and acclimatization at the high camps, and day 21 is summit day. The itinerary also has three spare days at Base Camp and a spare day in Kathmandu in case of bad weather.
What experience do you need to climb Ama Dablam?

The climb requires previous technical climbing experience, good fitness and adaptation to altitude, and it suits experienced climbers. On the ridge you ascend fixed ropes on a jumar and descend by rappelling on the rope, over rock, ice and mixed ground. A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure.
What is the Yellow Tower on Ama Dablam?

The Yellow Tower is a steep granite tower just below Camp 2, at almost 6,000 m, and it is the main technical section of the southwest ridge. Most climbers go up it on a jumar on a fixed rope, and Camp 2 sits on top of it.
How much does it cost to climb Ama Dablam?

The HighAir expedition costs 7,000 US dollars per person, and the price includes the flights to Lukla, accommodation, meals, a personal Sherpa guide, the fixed ropes, porters, the climbing permit and the entry permits. Not included are international flights, insurance, personal gear and climbing equipment, the Nepal visa (50 dollars), tips (350 dollars) and a summit bonus for the guides (800 dollars).
When is the season to climb Ama Dablam?
The main seasons are fall and spring, after and before the monsoon, and the fall is the busier of the two. Our expedition departs in October, after the monsoon season.
What language do the guides speak?
The expedition is led by professional local guides who speak English, and every climber has a personal Sherpa guide.
